newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African maize production costs up 15 pct y/y.
newsitem.headline: S.African maize production costs up 15 pct y/y.

text.p: South African maize production costs have risen by 15.5 percent this season compared with last year, the National Maize Producers Organisation (Nampo) said on Monday.

Giel van Zyl, general manager of Nampo, blamed the rise on price increases in diesel, which rose 36.1 percent, fertiliser, which went up by 24.2 percent, spare parts, which were up 18.2 percent, and crop insurance, up 20 percent.

Van Zyl said that based on an average crop yield of 2.5 tonnes per hectare over the past three years and faced with these increased production costs, maize farmers would need to receive a net price of 613 rand a tonne to break even.

"Against this background of sharp increases in the production cost of maize, the absence of a floor price and the size of the crop which is still unknown at this stage, producers must protect themselves as much as possible."
Van Zyl said forward contracts which were currently being closed at 550 rand a tonne would not ensure farmers a profit.
"For this reason producers must in all their transactions with buyers strive to obtain a price higher than 550 rand a tonne."
South Africa's maize market will from the start of the new season in May be free of a floor price for the first time in 70 years.
Nampo said a floor price was needed as the market was not sophisticated enough to use other hedging mechanisms, including futures and forward contracting.

The absence of support prices for farmers would lead to less maize being planted -- in a bid to prevent a surplus and low prices -- which could ultimately turn South Africa into a net importer of maize.
